lessons.title: Anchoring Phenomenon: Echoes at Hell's Gate, Ngong, Kisumu and Nairobi

quiz.prompt: Wanjiru and her friends shout towards a cliff at Hell's Gate and, after a short delay, hear their own voices come back. Which statement best describes what an echo is?
choices: Wind that carries the voice back to the listeners
A brand new sound that the cliff makes by itself
Sound that comes back to the listener after meeting a surface
A sound that the shouter's ears make after the shout
quiz.rationale: At this stage learners only need to recognise that an echo is sound coming back after meeting a surface. The other choices are common ideas, such as the wall making the sound or the wind carrying it back, which the class will test later.
quiz.placement: Predict: learners write what they think an echo is and share predictions with a partner

quiz.prompt: Before any teaching, Mr. Mwangi asks learners to write their own prediction about the echo. Why is it useful to write predictions first?
choices: So that learners with the same ideas as the teacher get the best marks
So that later evidence can be used to confirm, challenge or revise our ideas
So that the teacher can mark each prediction right or wrong straight away
So that the class never needs to change its ideas during the unit
quiz.rationale: Committing to an idea in writing lets learners compare it with evidence later and revise it. There are no right or wrong answers at this stage.
quiz.placement: Predict: individual written predictions, 'Our first ideas' recorded on the board

quiz.prompt: In the Echo Table, Hell's Gate has a cliff 85 m away and an echo delay of 0.50 s. Ngong Hills has a valley wall 170 m away and an echo delay of 1.00 s. Which statement correctly describes what the table shows for these two sites?
choices: Both sites have the same distance and the same delay
The Ngong wall is closer and its echo delay is longer
The Ngong wall is farther away but its echo delay is shorter
The Ngong wall is farther away and its echo delay is longer
quiz.rationale: Ngong has the larger distance (170 m compared with 85 m) and the larger delay (1.00 s compared with 0.50 s). Learners only describe this pattern and do not calculate anything yet.
quiz.placement: Part B: studying the Echo Table for the four trip sites

quiz.prompt: The Echo Table records what was heard at four sites. Which description matches the Kisumu school hall, where the far wall is 12 m away?
choices: A clear echo after a delay of 1.00 s
A clear echo after a delay of 0.50 s
No echo heard at all
A loud, muddy, drawn-out sound with a very short delay of 0.07 s
quiz.rationale: The table records the Kisumu hall as a loud, muddy and drawn-out sound with a delay of 0.07 s. This is different from the clear echoes at Hell's Gate and Ngong Hills and from the no-echo result in Nairobi.
quiz.placement: Part B: studying the Echo Table, comparing site C with sites A and B

quiz.prompt: On the open grounds of a Nairobi school, the nearest hard wall is 300 m away and learners hear no echo after shouting. At this point in the unit, which statement is the most scientific?
choices: The wind always blows the sound away, so there is no echo
The grass swallows the sound, so the matter is settled
The sound simply disappears once it is outside
We have observed that no echo is heard there, but we still need evidence from later lessons to explain why
quiz.rationale: The explanation has not been taught yet. Ideas such as 'grass swallows sound' or 'sound disappears' are first ideas to be tested, not conclusions, so the honest position is to describe what was observed and plan to investigate.
quiz.placement: Explain: pairs discuss why the Kisumu hall sounds muddy and the Nairobi field gives no echo

quiz.prompt: Which of these is the best question to add to the class Driving Question Board about the echo phenomenon?
choices: How many learners went on the trip?
Why does the Kisumu school hall sound muddy while the Hell's Gate cliff gives a clear echo?
Who in the group shouted first at the cliff?
What is the name of the national park in the story?
quiz.rationale: A good Driving Question Board question starts with Why or How, is about the phenomenon and can be investigated. The other questions ask for simple facts that do not help explain the echoes.
quiz.placement: DQB: learners write 2 or 3 questions on sticky notes and place them on the class Driving Question Board

quiz.prompt: Four learners draw their first echo models. Which drawing shows the most complete starting model of an echo?
choices: Only a person shouting, with no wall and no arrows
A person, a wall or cliff, and arrows showing sound going to the wall and coming back, with labels
Only a wall, with nothing showing where the sound comes from
A person and a wall with no arrows or labels
quiz.rationale: The initial model should show at least the source, a surface and a returning path, with labels. The other drawings are missing one or more of these parts.
quiz.placement: Model: each learner draws an Initial Echo Model with a source, a surface and a returning path

lessons.title: Rectilinear Propagation: Light and Wave Paths from Source to Cliff and Back

quiz.prompt: In an investigation, three cards each have a small hole at the same height. A torch shines at the first card and a screen is placed behind the third card. Light reaches the screen when the three holes are in a straight line. The middle card is then moved sideways so that its hole is off the line. What happens, and what does it show?
choices: The light bends around the card and still reaches the screen, showing light can curve
A dimmer spot of light still reaches the screen, showing light spreads in all directions around corners
The light reaches the screen but is brighter, showing light needs a bigger hole
No light reaches the screen, showing light travels in straight lines
quiz.rationale: Light passes only when the holes are aligned. When one hole is shifted the straight path is blocked, which is evidence for rectilinear propagation.
quiz.placement: Station 1 (Shadows): lining up three cards with holes and shifting the middle card

quiz.prompt: A pinhole camera is made from a tin with a small hole at one end and tracing paper at the other. It is pointed at a bright candle flame. The image of the flame on the tracing paper is upside down. Which explanation is correct?
choices: The tracing paper turns the image over
Light from the top of the flame travels in a straight line through the pinhole and lands at the bottom of the paper, and light from the bottom lands at the top
Light bends upwards after passing through the hole
The pinhole stores the light and releases it in reverse order
quiz.rationale: Straight rays from the top and bottom of the object cross at the pinhole, so the top of the object lands on the bottom of the screen. This supports straight-line travel of light.
quiz.placement: Station 2 (Pinhole camera): drawing lines from the top and bottom of the object through the pinhole to the screen

quiz.prompt: In Physics, what is a ray?
choices: The actual wave itself, which we can touch and see
A straight line with an arrow that shows the direction in which wave energy travels
A narrow shadow made by a torch behind an object
A curved line showing how a wave spreads out in all directions
quiz.rationale: A ray is a model: a straight line with an arrow showing the direction of energy travel. It is not the wave itself.
quiz.placement: Explain: agreeing on rectilinear propagation and defining a ray

quiz.prompt: The speed of light is 3.0 x 10^8 m/s and the speed of sound in air is 340 m/s. About how many times faster is light than sound?
choices: About 340 times
About 88 000 times
About 8 800 times
About 880 000 times
quiz.rationale: 3.0 x 10^8 / 340 is about 880 000, which is roughly 10^6 times faster.
quiz.placement: Explain: pairs calculate how many times faster light is than sound

quiz.prompt: Wanjiru shouts towards a cliff at Hell's Gate that is 85 m away. She hears her echo 0.50 s later. The speed of sound is 340 m/s. Which statement best explains the 0.50 s delay?
choices: The sound follows a curved path, which makes the journey slower
The sound takes 0.50 s to travel just the 85 m to the cliff, and returns instantly
The cliff stores the sound for a while and then releases it
The sound travels 85 m to the cliff and 85 m back, a total of 170 m, and this takes 0.50 s at 340 m/s
quiz.rationale: The sound travels out and back: 85 m + 85 m = 170 m. Time = 170 / 340 = 0.50 s. The delay is travel time, not storage by the cliff.
quiz.placement: Explain: drawing the Hell's Gate situation as a ray diagram, 85 m + 85 m = 170 m, 170 m / 340 m/s = 0.50 s

quiz.prompt: During a storm you see a lightning flash far away and hear the thunder a few seconds later. Why do you see the flash first?
choices: Light is louder than sound, so it is noticed first
Sound travels in a curved path, so it travels a longer distance than light
Light travels much faster than sound, so it reaches you almost instantly while sound takes time
The lightning makes the thunder only after the flash has ended
quiz.rationale: Light travels at about 3.0 x 10^8 m/s and sound at 340 m/s, so light arrives almost instantly and sound arrives later.
quiz.placement: Explain: comparing light and sound speeds and explaining why we see lightning before hearing thunder

quiz.prompt: A learner at Ngong Hills shouts towards a cliff 170 m away. The speed of sound is 340 m/s. How long is it before the learner hears the echo?
quiz.rationale: The sound travels 170 m to the cliff and 170 m back, a total of 340 m. Time = 340 / 340 = 1.00 s. The value 0.50 s is only the one-way time.
quiz.placement: Model: using the same ray idea for Ngong Hills (170 m, 1.00 s) on the class echo model

lessons.title: Reflection of Waves: The Laws of Reflection

quiz.prompt: A ray of light hits a plane mirror. The angle between the incoming ray and the normal is 40°. What angle will the reflected ray make with the normal?
quiz.rationale: By the first law of reflection, the angle of reflection r equals the angle of incidence i, and both are measured from the normal. So r = 40°.
quiz.placement: Predict: mirror prediction (ray at 40 degrees to the normal)

quiz.prompt: In a mirror experiment, Kiprono measures the angle between the incoming ray and the mirror surface and gets 50°. What is the angle of incidence i?
quiz.rationale: The angle of incidence is measured from the normal, which is at 90° to the mirror. So i = 90° - 50° = 40°.
quiz.placement: Station A: plane mirror (measuring i and r from the normal)

quiz.prompt: Straight ripples in a ripple tank travel towards a straight barrier that is tilted. What do the learners see after the ripples reach the barrier?
choices: The ripples bounce off at an angle equal to the angle at which they arrived, and stay straight
The ripples bend into circles and move in all directions
The ripples stop at the barrier and disappear
The ripples always return along exactly the same path, whatever the tilt
quiz.rationale: Water waves reflect from a barrier obeying the same law as light: the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence. The ripples change direction but keep their straight pattern.
quiz.placement: Station B: ripples (ripple tank or PhET simulation)

quiz.prompt: At a mirror, learners lay the incident ray, reflected ray and normal flat on paper. When they lift the torch slightly, the ray no longer stays on the paper. Which law of reflection does this check?
choices: The reflected ray is always on the same side of the normal as the incident ray
The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal lie in the same plane
The reflected ray is always shorter than the incident ray
The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection
quiz.rationale: When the ray is level with the paper, all three lines lie on one flat surface. This is the second law: the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in the same plane.
quiz.placement: Station A: plane mirror (checking the paper-plane and lifting the torch)

quiz.prompt: A sound ray from Kiprono hits the Hell's Gate cliff. The ray makes an angle of 30° with the surface of the cliff. What is the angle of reflection r, measured from the normal?
quiz.rationale: The angle of incidence is measured from the normal, which is at 90° to the cliff. So i = 90° - 30° = 60°, and r = i = 60°.
quiz.placement: Explain: applying the laws to Kiprono's sound ray at the Hell's Gate cliff (surface-angle probe)

quiz.prompt: Wanjiru shouts and part of her sound ray hits the cliff exactly along the normal (i = 0°). What happens to that ray after reflection?
choices: It continues straight through the cliff
It goes off at 90° to the cliff surface
It is absorbed by the cliff and a new sound is made
It returns along the same line it came from
quiz.rationale: If i = 0°, then r = 0° as well. The reflected ray leaves along the normal, so it goes back along its own path. Only a ray hitting along the normal returns along the same line.
quiz.placement: Explain: 'Does the sound need to come back along the same line it went?'

quiz.prompt: Amina draws a sound ray hitting a cliff at a point, with a dashed normal at that point. The incident ray makes an angle of 35° with the normal. Which drawing of the reflected ray is correct?
choices: On the same side of the normal as the incident ray, at 35° to the normal
Along the cliff surface, with no angle to the normal
On the opposite side of the normal, at 35° to the normal, going back towards the listener
On the opposite side of the normal, at 55° to the normal
quiz.rationale: The reflected ray lies on the opposite side of the normal from the incident ray, with r = i = 35°. It heads back towards the listener.
quiz.placement: Model: adding a reflection component to the class echo model (Hell's Gate scene)

lessons.title: Reflection of Sound: Echo Measurement and Surfaces

quiz.prompt: In the formula d = vt/2 used to find the distance to a wall from an echo, why is the time t divided by 2?
choices: The ear can only detect half of the time the sound travels
The speed of sound halves after it hits the wall
Only half of the sound energy reaches the wall
t is the time for the sound to go to the wall and come back, so the one-way distance uses half of it
quiz.rationale: The measured time t is for the round trip (to the wall and back). The distance to the wall is one way, so we use half the time, or half the total distance vt.
quiz.placement: Part A: calculating echo delays from the echo table with t = 2d/v

quiz.prompt: The ear can separate two sounds only if they are at least 0.1 s apart. Taking the speed of sound in air as 340 m/s, what is the minimum distance to a reflecting wall for a distinct echo?
quiz.rationale: The round trip must take at least 0.1 s, so d = vt/2 = 340 x 0.1 / 2 = 17 m. Forgetting to halve gives 34 m.
quiz.placement: Part A: deriving the minimum distance for a distinct echo (0.1 x 340 / 2 = 17 m)

quiz.prompt: A learner at a school in Nakuru claps and hears the echo 0.40 s later. The speed of sound is 340 m/s. How far away is the reflecting wall?
quiz.rationale: d = vt/2 = 340 x 0.40 / 2 = 68 m. The value 136 m is the round-trip distance, which is wrong because the wall is only half of that distance away.
quiz.placement: Part B: field measurement with d = vt/2 (and exit check on echo delay)

quiz.prompt: When measuring the echo distance with a stopwatch, a group times 10 clap-echo intervals and then divides by 10, instead of timing just one interval. Why do they do this?
choices: The speed of sound is only correct when 10 claps are used
The reaction-time error of starting and stopping the watch is spread over 10 intervals, so each interval is more accurate
The echo only becomes audible after 10 claps
The stopwatch works only for times longer than 1 second
quiz.rationale: Reaction time (about 0.2 s) is a big fraction of one short interval (about 0.3 s). Spread over 10 intervals, it becomes a small error in each one after dividing by 10.
quiz.placement: Part B: timing 10 clap-echo intervals at the school's long stone wall

quiz.prompt: A thick curtain reflects only 15% of the sound that hits it, while painted concrete reflects 85%. Which statement is correct?
choices: The curtain absorbs most of the sound energy and sends back a weak reflection
The curtain reflects more sound than concrete because it is thicker
Both surfaces reflect the same amount, but concrete is louder because it is heavier
The curtain reflects no sound at all, so it gives no echo
quiz.rationale: Soft surfaces like curtains absorb most of the sound energy (about 85%) but still reflect a small amount (15%). Hard smooth surfaces such as painted concrete reflect most of it.
quiz.placement: Part C: comparing the surface table (cliff rock 90%, painted concrete 85%, wooden board 60%, curtains 15%, grass or foam 10%)

quiz.prompt: On the open grounds of a Nairobi school covered with grass and bushes, the only large wall is 300 m away. A learner shouts and the calculated echo delay is 1.76 s, which is much longer than 0.1 s, yet no echo is heard. What is the best explanation?
choices: A delay longer than 0.1 s is too long for the ear to hear an echo
Sound cannot travel as far as 300 m in air
Grass and bushes absorb most of the sound and it spreads over a large area, so the returning sound is too faint to hear
The sound wave is destroyed when it hits a wall
quiz.rationale: The delay is 2 x 300 / 340 = 1.76 s, so time is not the problem. The grass reflects only about 10% and absorbs the rest, and the sound spreads out, so very little energy returns.
quiz.placement: Claim-evidence-reasoning for each site: why is the echo absent at site D

quiz.prompt: In a school hall in Kisumu with hard walls and a hard roof, a speaker 12 m from the far wall sounds loud, muddy and drawn out. What is the best explanation?
choices: Sound travels more slowly inside buildings than outside
Sound reflects many times from the hard surfaces and the reflections overlap and merge, which is called reverberation
The hall walls absorb all the sound, so it takes longer to fade
The far wall is more than 17 m away, so the echo comes back too late to be heard
quiz.rationale: The 12 m distance gives a delay of only about 0.07 s, less than 0.1 s. Repeated reflections from hard surfaces overlap and merge with the original sound, prolonging it (reverberation).
quiz.placement: Claim-evidence-reasoning for each site: why the Kisumu hall is muddy (echo versus reverberation)

quiz.prompt: A learner stands 40 m from a wall completely covered with thick curtains and claps. The speed of sound is 340 m/s. Which prediction is best?
choices: A loud echo, because the delay is longer than 0.1 s
No echo at all, because the wall is too close
A separate but weak echo, because the delay is about 0.24 s but the curtains absorb most of the sound
No sound returns, because curtains reflect 0%
quiz.rationale: The delay is 2 x 40 / 340 = 0.24 s, which is more than 0.1 s, and 40 m is more than 17 m, so the echo would be separate. The curtains reflect only about 15%, so the echo is weak.
quiz.placement: Revising the class echo model: test case with a curtained wall 40 m away

lessons.title: Refraction of Waves: Why Waves Change Direction When Their Speed Changes

quiz.prompt: Amina puts a straw in a glass of water and it looks broken at the water surface. Which statement best explains why?
choices: Water magnifies the straw so the part under water looks closer.
The straw really bends when it is put into water.
Light from the straw changes speed and direction as it passes between water and air.
Light reflects off the water surface and bounces back to the eye.
quiz.rationale: Light travels at different speeds in water and in air, so it changes direction at the surface (refraction). The straw is not physically bent, and this is not reflection.
quiz.placement: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) statement about the bent straw

quiz.prompt: Light travels at 3.0 x 10^8 m/s in air and 2.26 x 10^8 m/s in water. A ray of light goes from air into water at an angle. What happens to it?
choices: It speeds up and bends away from the normal.
It slows down and bends toward the normal.
It slows down and bends away from the normal.
It keeps the same speed and does not bend.
quiz.rationale: 2.26 x 10^8 m/s is less than 3.0 x 10^8 m/s, so light slows down entering water. A wave that slows down bends toward the normal.
quiz.placement: Complete the sentence: 'Light is slower in water (2.26 x 10^8 m/s) than in air... so it bends ___ the normal when entering water'

quiz.prompt: Sound travels at 340 m/s in air and about 1500 m/s in water. A sound wave moves from air into water at an angle. What happens to it?
choices: It speeds up and bends toward the normal.
It speeds up and bends away from the normal.
It keeps the same speed but changes direction.
It slows down because water is denser, and bends toward the normal.
quiz.rationale: Sound is faster in water (1500 m/s) than in air (340 m/s), so it speeds up and bends away from the normal. The idea that denser water always slows waves is a misconception, because it applies to light but not to sound.
quiz.placement: Compare sound: 'Sound goes from 340 m/s in air to 1500 m/s in water, so it speeds up and bends ___ the normal'

quiz.prompt: A Lake Victoria shallow pool has a real depth of 1.33 m. Water has a refractive index of 1.33, so the apparent depth equals the real depth divided by 1.33. How deep does the pool look when viewed from directly above?
quiz.rationale: Apparent depth = real depth / 1.33 = 1.33 / 1.33 = 1.00 m. Rays from the bottom bend away from the normal as they leave the water, so the pool looks shallower than it really is.
quiz.placement: Station 2: Apparent depth (coin in the cup) and the data card with the Lake Victoria pool

quiz.prompt: A learner looks straight down at a straw standing in a cup of water, along the normal to the water surface. What does the learner see, and what happens to the light speed?
choices: The straw looks bent, because light changes speed in water.
The straw looks straight, but light still changes speed in water.
The straw looks bent, because light changes direction but not speed.
The straw looks straight, because light does not change speed along the normal.
quiz.rationale: Light entering along the normal is not bent, so the straw looks straight. Its speed still changes in the new medium, because bending depends on the angle of approach but the speed depends on the medium.
quiz.placement: Station 1: Bent straw, viewing from directly above (along the normal)

quiz.prompt: Water waves in a ripple tank move from deep water into shallow water, where they travel more slowly. The frequency stays the same. What happens to the waves?
choices: The wavelength becomes shorter but the wave fronts stay straight in their original direction.
The wavelength becomes shorter and the wave fronts bend.
The wavelength becomes longer and the wave fronts bend.
The wavelength stays the same and the wave fronts bend.
quiz.rationale: Speed = frequency x wavelength. With the frequency fixed and the speed smaller, the wavelength is shorter. The part of the wave front that enters the shallow water first slows down first, so the wave front swings and changes direction.
quiz.placement: Station 3: Offline video of a ripple tank with water waves moving from deep to shallow water

quiz.prompt: A shout from Hell's Gate hits a cliff face and part of the sound returns as an echo. The rest goes into the rock. Which statement correctly describes what the wave does at this boundary?
choices: The returning part is reflected and stays in the air with i = r. The part entering the rock is refracted, with a new speed and direction.
All of the sound is reflected, so none of it can be refracted.
The returning part is refracted, and the part entering the rock is reflected.
Both parts are refracted, because every wave changes direction at a boundary.
quiz.rationale: Reflection sends a wave back into the first medium with i = r, which makes the echo. Refraction is the part that goes on into the second medium at a different speed and direction.
quiz.placement: Adding refraction to the class echo model: the reflected wave and the refracted wave at a boundary

lessons.title: Snell's Law, Refractive Index and Lenses: Bending Waves in Our Echo Model

quiz.prompt: A thin ray of light in air hits the surface of water at 45 degrees from the normal. What happens to the ray as it enters the water?
choices: It bends away from the normal, so the angle in water is more than 45 degrees
It bends towards the surface of the water, so the angle from the normal stays at 45 degrees
It bends towards the normal, so the angle in water is less than 45 degrees
It goes straight on without bending
quiz.rationale: Water has a higher refractive index than air (1.33 against 1.00), so light slows down and bends towards the normal. Learners measured about 32 degrees from the normal in water.
quiz.placement: Station 1: Refraction (glass block and water container, i = 45 degrees)

quiz.prompt: A ray in air (n = 1.00) hits water (n = 1.33) at i = 45 degrees. Use n1 sin i = n2 sin r with sin 45 = 0.707. What is the value of sin r?
quiz.rationale: 1.00 x 0.707 = 1.33 x sin r, so sin r = 0.707 / 1.33 = 0.532, which gives r = 32 degrees. Multiplying by 1.33 instead of dividing gives 0.941, and dividing by 1.50 gives 0.471, which is the glass value.
quiz.placement: Station 1: Refraction (calculate with Snell's law and compare with measured r)

quiz.prompt: The speed of light in air is 3.0 x 10^8 m/s. Glass has a refractive index of 1.50. Using n = c/v, what is the speed of light in glass?
quiz.rationale: v = c/n = 3.0 x 10^8 / 1.50 = 2.0 x 10^8 m/s. Light is slower in glass than in air, so the answer cannot be bigger than 3.0 x 10^8 m/s.
quiz.placement: Explain: practice problem 2 (find the speed of light in glass)

quiz.prompt: Kiprono says glass bends light more than water because glass is harder. Which is the correct scientific reason that light bends more in glass than in water?
choices: Glass reflects most of the light, so the rest is bent more
Glass is solid, and solids always bend light more than liquids
Light travels faster in glass than in water, so it is pulled more towards the normal
Light travels more slowly in glass (n = 1.50) than in water (n = 1.33), so it bends more towards the normal
quiz.rationale: A higher refractive index means slower light, and a bigger drop in speed gives more bending towards the normal. Hardness is not the cause of the bending.
quiz.placement: Explain: building the explanation using speeds (n = c/v)

quiz.prompt: Parallel rays of light from a torch pass through a converging (convex) lens and then through a diverging (concave) lens. Which statement describes what each lens does to the rays?
choices: Both lenses bring the rays together at a focal point
Both lenses spread the rays out, but by different amounts
The converging lens spreads the rays out, and the diverging lens brings them to a focal point
The converging lens brings the rays together at a focal point, and the diverging lens spreads them as if they came from a focal point behind the lens
quiz.rationale: A converging lens makes parallel rays meet at a focal point. A diverging lens spreads them so they appear to come from a focal point behind the lens.
quiz.placement: Station 2: Lenses (converging and diverging lens ray diagrams)

quiz.prompt: A learner in a Kisumu classroom can read a book clearly but cannot read the board from the back of the class. This is short sight. Which lens would help, and why?
choices: A converging lens, because it spreads the rays slightly
A diverging lens, because it spreads the rays slightly so that the image falls on the retina
No lens can help, because the problem is in the board and not in the eye
A converging lens, because it brings distant rays together more strongly
quiz.rationale: Short sight is corrected with a diverging lens, which spreads the rays a little so that the image forms on the retina. Converging lenses are used to correct long sight.
quiz.placement: Explain: connecting lenses to uses (spectacles, short and long sight)

quiz.prompt: At Hell's Gate, learners shout at a cliff and hear their voices return after 0.50 s. Which statement correctly explains the returning shout?
choices: The sound wave is refracted by the cliff, and the bending sends it back to the learners
The sound wave is reflected from the cliff, and reflection is what sends the wave back; refraction describes only the part that enters the cliff material
Refraction and reflection are the same process, so either word can explain the echo
The sound wave enters the cliff and Snell's law makes it come back out towards the learners
quiz.rationale: An echo is a reflected wave that returns to the listener. Refraction describes the part of a wave that goes into a new medium and bends there. It does not by itself explain the echo.
quiz.placement: Model: revising the class echo model (key box: reflection returns the wave, refraction bends the wave that enters)

lessons.title: Diffraction of Waves: Why Sound Turns Corners but Light Does Not

quiz.prompt: Wanjiru can hear Mr. Mwangi calling from around the corner of the classroom block, but she cannot see him. Which explanation is best?
choices: Sound waves spread round edges and through gaps much more than light, because their wavelength is far larger
Sound is louder than light, so it can get round corners
Sound travels only in straight lines, but it bounces off the walls
Light is too fast to bend round corners, but sound is slow enough to bend
quiz.rationale: Sound has a wavelength of about 1 m, comparable to doorways and building edges, so it diffracts strongly. Light has a wavelength of about 5.5 x 10^-7 m, far smaller than the gap, so it barely bends.
quiz.placement: Predict: learners gather round the 1.0 m classroom door while Mr. Mwangi speaks out of sight and a torch is shone through the doorway

quiz.prompt: The speed of sound in air is 340 m/s. What is the wavelength of a sound of frequency 1000 Hz?
quiz.rationale: Use lambda = v / f = 340 / 1000 = 0.34 m.
quiz.placement: Observe: calculating wavelengths using v = f x wavelength (340 Hz and 1000 Hz sounds)

quiz.prompt: In a ripple tank, plane waves of wavelength 1.0 m (scaled) meet a barrier with a gap. Only the gap width is changed. Which gap width will give the strongest spreading of the waves on the far side?
choices: A gap of 1.0 m
A gap of 20 m
A gap of 5 m
A gap of 100 m
quiz.rationale: Diffraction is greatest when the gap is comparable to the wavelength. A 1.0 m gap equals the 1.0 m wavelength, while the other gaps are much wider than the wavelength and give little spreading.
quiz.placement: Observe: Task A, changing the gap width in the PhET Wave Interference simulation and recording the amount of spreading

quiz.prompt: A doorway is 1.0 m wide. Green light has a wavelength of 5.5 x 10^-7 m. About how many light wavelengths fit across the doorway?
choices: About 550
About 1 818 182 (1.8 million)
About 5.5
quiz.rationale: Number of wavelengths = gap / wavelength = 1.0 / 5.5 x 10^-7 = about 1.8 million. The gap is enormously larger than the wavelength, so light shows almost no visible bending.
quiz.placement: Observe: data table comparing the 1.0 m gap with light of wavelength 5.5 x 10^-7 m

quiz.prompt: Sound of frequency 340 Hz and sound of frequency 1000 Hz (speed 340 m/s) pass through a doorway 1.0 m wide. Which statement is correct?
choices: The 1000 Hz sound spreads more, because a higher frequency means more energy
The 340 Hz sound spreads more, because its wavelength of 1.0 m is comparable to the doorway width
Both spread equally, because the gap is the same for both
The 1000 Hz sound spreads more, because its wavelength of 0.34 m is smaller than the gap
quiz.rationale: The 340 Hz sound has lambda = 340/340 = 1.0 m, equal to the gap, so it spreads strongly. The 1000 Hz sound has lambda = 0.34 m, so the gap is about 3 wavelengths and the spreading is less. This is why low sounds such as matatu bass are heard round corners better.
quiz.placement: Explain: applying the idea to a new situation (340 Hz versus 1000 Hz sound heard around a corner) and the exit-ticket question

quiz.prompt: A 340 Hz sound wave passes through a doorway and spreads out into the corridor beyond. What happens to the frequency and wavelength of the sound because of this diffraction?
choices: The frequency becomes lower and the pitch drops
The wavelength becomes longer and the frequency stays the same
The frequency and the wavelength both stay the same
The frequency increases because the wave is squeezed through the gap
quiz.rationale: Diffraction changes the direction in which the wave travels and spreads, but it does not change the frequency or wavelength of the wave, so the pitch stays the same.
quiz.placement: Explain: teacher question 'Does diffraction change the speed or the pitch of the sound?'

quiz.prompt: A learner shouts on a large open school field. The sound gets weaker as it travels away in all directions, so no echo is heard. What is the best explanation for the sound becoming weaker?
choices: The wavelength of the sound gets shorter as the wave travels
Diffraction destroys part of the wave's energy at the edges
The frequency of the sound drops as it moves across open ground
The wave spreads out in all directions, so the same energy covers a bigger area; this is different from diffraction
quiz.rationale: As a shout spreads out in all directions its energy covers a larger area, so it gets weaker. This is ordinary spreading out, not diffraction, which is the bending of waves round edges and through gaps and does not change wavelength or frequency.
quiz.placement: Model: revising the class echo model to show the shout spreading across the open Nairobi grounds, and keeping this separate from diffraction

lessons.title: Interference of Waves: When Sound Waves Meet in the Kisumu Hall

quiz.prompt: In a ripple tank, two dippers touch the water at the same rate. Along some lines the water surface stays nearly flat, even though both dippers are still moving. What is happening along those lines?
choices: The waves from the two dippers always add to make bigger waves, so the flat water is a mistake
The dippers are not sending any waves in those directions
The waves from the two dippers bounce off each other and stop
A crest from one dipper meets a trough from the other, so their displacements add up to almost zero
quiz.rationale: When waves meet, their displacements add (superposition). Where a crest meets a trough they cancel, which is destructive interference, so the water stays nearly flat.
quiz.placement: Observe, Station 1: ripple tank (or LabXchange: Wave Interference simulation)

quiz.prompt: Two speakers play the same note of frequency 340 Hz. The speed of sound in air is 340 m/s. What is the wavelength of the sound?
quiz.rationale: Use v = f x wavelength, so wavelength = v / f = 340 / 340 = 1.0 m.
quiz.placement: Observe, Station 2: PhET Sound simulation with two speakers set to 340 Hz (confirming lambda = 340/340 = 1.0 m)

quiz.prompt: Two speakers play a 340 Hz note, so the wavelength is 1.0 m. A learner stands 5.0 m from one speaker and 5.5 m from the other. What is the path difference, and what does the learner hear?
choices: 10.5 m, which is a whole number of wavelengths, so the sound is loud
5.5 m, which is more than one wavelength, so the sound is loud
0.5 m, which is half a wavelength, so the sound is quiet
0.5 m, which is half a wavelength, so the sound is loud
quiz.rationale: Path difference = 5.5 - 5.0 = 0.5 m, which is half a wavelength (0.5/1.0). Crest meets trough, so destructive interference gives a quiet spot.
quiz.placement: Explain: worked example (speakers at 340 Hz, listener 5.0 m and 5.5 m away)

quiz.prompt: Two speakers play a 340 Hz note, so the wavelength is 1.0 m. A listener stands where the path difference from the two speakers is 2.0 m. What does the listener hear, and why?
choices: Quiet, because a larger path difference always makes the sound weaker
Loud, because 2.0 m is half a wavelength
Quiet, because the waves from the two speakers cancel whenever the path difference is more than 1.0 m
Loud, because 2.0 m is two whole wavelengths, so crest meets crest
quiz.rationale: A path difference of 2.0 m is 2.0 / 1.0 = 2 whole wavelengths. The waves are in step, so constructive interference gives a loud sound.
quiz.placement: Explain: deciding what would happen at path difference 2.0 m (loud)

quiz.prompt: A learner walking across a room between two speakers playing the same note finds a quiet spot. Both speakers are still switched on. Which statement best explains the quiet spot?
choices: The waves from both speakers still arrive, but a crest from one meets a trough from the other and they cancel at that point
The air at that spot blocks the sound from both speakers
One of the speakers has stopped working
The sound energy is destroyed completely and cannot be found anywhere in the room
quiz.rationale: Both waves still reach the spot, but their displacements cancel when they are half a wavelength out of step. The energy is not destroyed; it is redistributed to the loud places.
quiz.placement: Explain: whole-class sensemaking (the rule in learners' own words) and Observe, Station 3: Kiprono's challenge (loud and quiet spots)

quiz.prompt: In the Kisumu school hall, the far wall is 12 m away and the echo delay is 0.07 s, which is less than 0.1 s. Which statement about the sound in the hall is correct?
choices: All the reflected waves cancel each other everywhere, so the hall should be silent
The waves collide and stop, so the sound cannot reach the seats at the back
The hall has no reflections, so the sound is loud only because of the speaker
Reflected waves from the walls, floor and roof overlap with the original sound and add in some places and partly cancel in others
quiz.rationale: The echo arrives less than 0.1 s after the original, so reflected and direct waves overlap. They add in some places (loud) and partly cancel in others (quiet), which makes the sound loud and muddy.
quiz.placement: Explain: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning, applying interference to the Kisumu hall (site C)

quiz.prompt: A noise-cancelling headphone must cancel a steady 340 Hz engine noise. The speed of sound is 340 m/s, so the wavelength of the noise is 1.0 m. How far out of step must the wave made by the headphone be?
choices: 1.0 m, which is one whole wavelength out of step
0 m, so the wave is exactly in step with the noise
0.5 m, which is half a wavelength out of step
340 m, which is the speed of sound
quiz.rationale: For destructive interference, the second wave must be half a wavelength out of step: 1.0 / 2 = 0.5 m. Then crest meets trough at the ear and the noise cancels.
quiz.placement: Explain: noise-cancelling headphones (bus engine rumble from Kisumu to Nairobi)

quiz.prompt: At Hell's Gate, a cliff 85 m away gives a clean echo after 0.50 s. In the Kisumu hall the sound is muddy. Which is the best reason for the difference?
choices: Sound travels faster in the open air, so no waves can meet
At Hell's Gate there is a single reflection arriving after a clear delay, so there is little overlap, while in the hall many reflections overlap
At Hell's Gate the reflected waves always cancel the original sound
At Hell's Gate the cliff does not reflect sound
quiz.rationale: The cliff gives one clean reflection after 0.50 s, so it hardly overlaps the original shout. In the hall, many reflections arrive close together and overlap, adding and cancelling at different places.
quiz.placement: Model: Hell's Gate panel (85 m, 0.50 s, single clean reflection) beside the Kisumu hall diagram

lessons.title: Stationary Waves and Resonance: Nodes, Antinodes and the Pitch of the Nyatiti and Flute

quiz.prompt: A nyatiti string is fixed at both ends. A wave travelling along the string reaches one fixed end. What does the wave do there?
choices: It stops and stays at the end of the string
It speeds up and leaves the string
It is reflected and travels back along the string
It disappears at the end and is lost
quiz.rationale: As with an echo from a cliff, a wave reaching a fixed end is reflected and travels back. This reflected wave later meets the incoming wave.
quiz.placement: Predict: learners sketch the plucked nyatiti string and complete 'When a wave reaches the fixed end of the string, I think it ...'

quiz.prompt: A 0.60 m nyatiti string vibrates in its second harmonic (two loops). How many nodes (counting both fixed ends) and how many antinodes does the stationary wave have?
choices: 2 nodes and 2 antinodes
2 nodes and 3 antinodes
3 nodes and 2 antinodes
4 nodes and 3 antinodes
quiz.rationale: Two loops give 2 antinodes, one in the middle of each loop. The nodes are at the two ends and in the middle, giving 3 nodes. A node is a point of zero amplitude and an antinode is a point of maximum amplitude.
quiz.placement: Observe, Station A and Station B: recording loops, nodes (including ends) and antinodes for the fundamental and second harmonic

quiz.prompt: Why does a vibrating string show a stationary wave pattern that stays in place instead of a wave that travels along it?
choices: Two waves travelling in the same direction add up to give a bigger wave
The string stops the wave from moving when it is plucked
Plucking the string harder makes the wave stay in one place
The wave and its reflection travel in opposite directions and superpose, adding at antinodes and cancelling at nodes
quiz.rationale: The incident wave and the wave reflected from the fixed end travel in opposite directions and interfere. They add (constructive) at antinodes and cancel (destructive) at nodes, so the pattern stays in place.
quiz.placement: Explain, Step 1: why a pattern forms (reflection at the fixed end plus superposition)

quiz.prompt: A nyatiti string has a vibrating length of 0.60 m. The wave speed on the string is 120 m/s. What is the frequency of the fundamental (one loop)?
choices: 100 Hz
200 Hz
50 Hz
144 Hz
quiz.rationale: For the fundamental, wavelength = 2L = 2 x 0.60 = 1.20 m. Then f = v/wavelength = 120/1.20 = 100 Hz. Using L instead of 2L as the wavelength gives the wrong value of 200 Hz.
quiz.placement: Explain, Step 3: nyatiti calculation (L = 0.60 m, v = 120 m/s)

quiz.prompt: A flute is modelled as an open tube of length 0.34 m. The speed of sound in air is 340 m/s. What is the frequency of its fundamental note?
choices: 250 Hz
500 Hz
116 Hz
quiz.rationale: For the fundamental in an open tube, wavelength = 2L = 2 x 0.34 = 0.68 m. Then f = v/wavelength = 340/0.68 = 500 Hz. Taking the wavelength as L gives the wrong value of 1000 Hz.
quiz.placement: Explain, Step 3: flute calculation (open tube L = 0.34 m, v = 340 m/s)

quiz.prompt: A nyatiti player presses a string against the neck so that the vibrating length becomes shorter. What happens to the note?
choices: The pitch stays the same but the note is louder
The pitch depends only on how hard the string is plucked
The frequency is lower, so the pitch is lower
The frequency is higher, so the pitch is higher
quiz.rationale: A shorter string has a shorter wavelength (wavelength = 2L), so with the same wave speed the frequency f = v/2L is higher. Pitch depends on frequency, while loudness depends on amplitude.
quiz.placement: Explain: pitch depends on frequency, and a shorter string or tube gives a higher pitch

quiz.prompt: In a school hall in Kisumu with hard walls, some notes sound extra loud and boom, while others do not. Which explanation fits best?
choices: The echo of those notes takes longer to come back
Louder notes always have a higher frequency
The frequency of those notes matches a natural frequency of the hall, so the vibration grows large (resonance)
Sound waves stop completely at nodes, so the other notes are lost
quiz.rationale: Resonance happens when a driving frequency matches a natural frequency of the system. The reflections in the hall then reinforce that note and the amplitude becomes large. Loudness depends on amplitude, not on frequency.
quiz.placement: DQB: 'Which of our earlier questions about the muddy Kisumu hall does resonance help with?'

lessons.title: Doppler Effect: Why the Ambulance Siren Changes Pitch as It Passes

quiz.prompt: An ambulance siren always produces a steady 700 Hz note. As the ambulance passes a bus, the people in the bus hear the pitch drop. Which explanation is correct?
choices: The siren becomes louder as it comes closer, and loudness is the same as pitch
The wind speeds up the sound as the ambulance goes past
The siren changes to a lower note as the ambulance passes
Because the ambulance is moving, the number of sound waves reaching the ear each second changes, so the pitch heard changes
quiz.rationale: The siren itself stays at 700 Hz. The motion of the source changes how often wavefronts reach the listener. Loudness and pitch are different things.
quiz.placement: Predict: learners write a prediction about the ambulance siren on Waiyaki Way and sketch the waves in front of and behind it

quiz.prompt: A parked ambulance sounds its siren at 700 Hz. The speed of sound in air is 340 m/s. Using v = f x wavelength, what is the wavelength of the siren sound?
quiz.rationale: wavelength = v / f = 340 / 700 = 0.486 m. Dividing the other way round (700/340) gives 2.06 m, which is wrong.
quiz.placement: Observe: learners study the ambulance data table and calculate the wavelength of the 700 Hz siren at rest

quiz.prompt: In a scale model of a moving siren, Amina walks steadily along a line at 0.5 m/s while a timekeeper claps once every second. Each clap's wavefront travels outwards at 1 m/s. Otieno stands ahead of Amina and Wanjiru stands behind her. The wavefronts are 0.5 m apart in front of Amina and 1.5 m apart behind her. Who receives wavefronts more often, and why?
choices: Otieno, because the wavefronts ahead of Amina are closer together, so more of them reach him each second
Otieno, because Amina claps faster when she walks towards him
Wanjiru, because the wavefronts behind Amina are further apart and carry more energy
Both receive them equally often, because Amina claps once every second
quiz.rationale: Wavefronts are bunched up ahead of the moving source (0.5 m apart), so about 2 reach Otieno each second. Behind the source they are stretched out, so fewer reach Wanjiru. The clapping rate stays the same.
quiz.placement: Explain: scale model walk with Amina as the siren, wavefront circles drawn with string and chalk or a compass

quiz.prompt: An ambulance siren emits 700 Hz. The ambulance moves towards you at 20 m/s and the speed of sound is 340 m/s. Using observed frequency = 700 x 340 / (340 - 20), what frequency do you hear?
choices: 720 Hz
744 Hz
700 Hz
661 Hz
quiz.rationale: f = 700 x 340 / (340 - 20) = 238 000 / 320 = about 744 Hz. This is higher than 700 Hz because the waves are bunched up in front of the approaching source.
quiz.placement: Explain: learners use the data to work out the approaching frequency of 744 Hz

quiz.prompt: An ambulance with a 700 Hz siren drives away from you. A learner says: 'The sound must now travel more slowly, which is why the pitch is lower.' Which statement correctly describes what happens?
choices: The speed of sound drops below 340 m/s, so the frequency drops
The speed of sound stays at 340 m/s, the waves behind the ambulance are stretched out, so the wavelength is longer and the frequency heard is lower
The siren frequency drops because the engine is further away
The speed of sound stays at 340 m/s, the waves are bunched up, so the frequency heard is lower
quiz.rationale: The speed of sound in air does not change when the source moves. Wavefronts behind a receding source are stretched out (longer wavelength), so fewer reach the listener each second, giving a lower frequency (661 Hz in the example).
quiz.placement: Explain: CER statement and discussion of why the bottom number is 340 plus 20 for receding

quiz.prompt: A traffic officer on a Nairobi highway uses a radar speed gun. How does the gun find the speed of a moving matatu?
choices: It measures the colour of the matatu using light waves
It sends radio waves at the matatu and measures how much the frequency of the reflected waves has shifted
It measures only how long a sound takes to return, which does not depend on speed
It measures how loud the matatu's engine sounds
quiz.rationale: The radar gun uses the Doppler effect: the reflected radio waves from a moving vehicle return with a shifted frequency, and the size of the shift gives the speed.
quiz.placement: Explain: Mr. Mwangi introduces uses of the Doppler effect (radar speed gun and redshift)

quiz.prompt: At the Kisumu school hall, a shout gives a muddy, drawn-out echo. A learner says the Doppler effect explains the muddy echo. Which reply is correct?
choices: Yes, because the hall makes the pitch of the shout higher
No, the muddy echo comes from many overlapping reflections, while the Doppler effect is about motion changing the frequency
Yes, because the sound is travelling at a changing speed in the hall
No, because the Doppler effect only happens outdoors
quiz.rationale: A muddy echo is caused by overlapping reflections arriving close together. The Doppler effect needs relative motion between source and observer and changes pitch.
quiz.placement: DQB: learners link Doppler to echoes and discuss whether Doppler explains why the Kisumu hall is muddy

quiz.prompt: At Hell's Gate, the cliff does not move, so the echo of a shout has the same pitch as the shout. What would make the pitch of the returning echo change?
choices: The shouter and the cliff moving towards or away from each other
The echo taking longer to return
The shout being louder
The cliff being taller
quiz.rationale: Relative motion between the sound source and the reflecting surface changes the observed frequency. Delay, height of the cliff and loudness do not change the pitch.
quiz.placement: Model: adding the Doppler panel and the note about a moving reflector or source to the class echo model

lessons.title: Waves in Communication and Medicine: FM Radio and Ultrasound as Echo Applications

quiz.prompt: Wanjiru listens to an FM radio station broadcast from a studio in Nairobi while she is in Kericho. What carries the station's signal through the space between the transmitter and her radio?
choices: Ultrasound pulses sent from the studio to the radio
Sound waves travelling through the air at about 340 m/s
Echoes of the announcer's voice bouncing between hills
Electromagnetic (radio) waves travelling at 3.0 x 10^8 m/s, which need no medium
quiz.rationale: Radio waves are electromagnetic waves. They travel at 3.0 x 10^8 m/s and need no medium, so the signal is not ordinary sound moving through air.
quiz.placement: Predict Phase: how a voice from a studio in Nairobi reaches a radio far away

quiz.prompt: A doctor uses ultrasound to scan a patient at a county hospital. What does the word 'ultrasound' mean?
choices: Sound that travels only through air and cannot enter the body
A high-frequency radio wave that travels at 3.0 x 10^8 m/s
Sound with a frequency above the range of human hearing, which is about 20 000 Hz
Sound that is extremely loud but still within the range of human hearing
quiz.rationale: Ultrasound is sound whose frequency is above what humans can hear. It is not extra-loud sound and it is not an electromagnetic wave.
quiz.placement: Predict Phase: how a doctor can use sound we cannot hear to find an organ boundary

quiz.prompt: An FM station broadcasts at a carrier frequency of 91.0 MHz. Radio waves travel at 3.0 x 10^8 m/s. What is the wavelength of the carrier wave? (1 MHz = 1 000 000 Hz)
quiz.rationale: Wavelength = v / f = 3.0 x 10^8 / (91.0 x 10^6) = 3.30 m. The other values come from slipping the power of ten or inverting the formula.
quiz.placement: Part A: FM radio, calculating the wavelength of the 91.0 MHz carrier

quiz.prompt: In FM (frequency modulation) radio, a voice is carried by the radio wave. What does the voice signal change in the carrier wave?
choices: The speed of the carrier, which becomes 340 m/s
The height (amplitude) of the carrier, while its frequency stays the same
The carrier frequency, which is squeezed and stretched, while the amplitude stays the same
Nothing, because the radio wave carries the sound itself as air vibrations
quiz.rationale: In FM the voice signal makes the carrier frequency go up and down slightly, while the amplitude stays constant. The radio then changes these variations back into sound.
quiz.placement: Part A: FM radio, looking at the graphs of a carrier wave and a voice signal

quiz.prompt: An ultrasound probe sends a pulse into soft tissue, where the speed of ultrasound is 1540 m/s. A tissue boundary is 7.7 cm (0.077 m) deep. After how long does the echo from the boundary return to the probe?
choices: 1000 microseconds
50 microseconds
453 microseconds
100 microseconds
quiz.rationale: The pulse travels to the boundary and back, so t = 2d / v = 2 x 0.077 / 1540 = 1.0 x 10^-4 s = 100 microseconds. Forgetting the factor 2 gives 50 microseconds, and using 340 m/s gives about 453 microseconds.
quiz.placement: Part B: Ultrasound, using d = vt/2 for the 7.7 cm boundary

quiz.prompt: A 3.5 MHz ultrasound probe in soft tissue has a wavelength of about 0.44 mm. Why can a doctor use this ultrasound, but not a loud shout like the one at Hell's Gate, to find small boundaries inside the body?
choices: Sound that we can hear cannot reflect from anything inside the body
A shout is too loud and would break the tissue, while ultrasound is quiet
Ultrasound travels faster than light, so it returns before the shout does
The wavelength of audible sound is too long to show small detail, while the 0.44 mm wavelength of ultrasound suits small boundaries
quiz.rationale: Audible sound has wavelengths far too long to reveal small features. Ultrasound has a wavelength of only 0.44 mm, so it can show fine detail. Loudness and speed are not the reason.
quiz.placement: Explain Phase: why a doctor cannot use the Hell's Gate shout to scan a body

quiz.prompt: At Hell's Gate a shout reflects from a cliff 85 m away and returns after 0.50 s. An ultrasound pulse reflects from a tissue boundary 7.7 cm deep and returns after 100 microseconds. Which statement correctly compares the two echoes?
choices: Both echoes take the same time, because the speed of sound is the same in air and in tissue
Both use reflection and the same relation d = vt/2, but the wave speed, distance and time are different
Hell's Gate uses d = vt/2, but ultrasound uses d = vt because it is a different kind of wave
Ultrasound does not reflect, so the timing method used at Hell's Gate cannot work for it
quiz.rationale: Both are reflections where the wave travels there and back, so d = vt/2 applies. Only the speed (about 340 m/s in air, 1540 m/s in tissue), the distance and the time change.
quiz.placement: Model Phase: adding the 'Technology' branch with arrows back to Hell's Gate, and the exit slip on similarity and difference

lessons.title: Noise Pollution and the Final Model: Why Do Some Places Echo and Others Do Not?

quiz.prompt: The class safe limit is 85 dB for up to 8 hours. Which of these sources is ABOVE the safe limit?
choices: Matatu with loud music (95 dB)
Kisumu hall during assembly (85 dB)
Ordinary conversation (60 dB)
Whisper (30 dB)
quiz.rationale: 95 dB is greater than 85 dB, so the matatu with loud music is above the limit. The Kisumu hall at 85 dB is exactly at the limit, and the other two are well below it.
quiz.placement: Part 1 (decibel data): bar chart with the 85 dB line

quiz.prompt: In the Kisumu hall, the far wall is 12 m away and the speed of sound is 340 m/s. Which statement gives the correct delay and what it means?
choices: 0.04 s, because the sound travels 12 m, so it is heard as a clear separate echo
28 s, because the sound is delayed a long time before it returns
0.07 s, which is less than 0.1 s, so the reflected sound merges with the original voice
0.07 s, which is more than 0.1 s, so it is heard as a clear separate echo
quiz.rationale: The sound travels there and back, so t = 2d/v = 24/340 = 0.07 s. This is less than 0.1 s, so the ear cannot separate the reflection from the original sound, and repeated reflections make it muddy (reverberation).
quiz.placement: Part 3 (calculation link): site C round trip 24 m, t = 2d/v

quiz.prompt: A school hall has hard painted concrete walls that reflect 85% of sound. Curtains reflect only 15% and foam only 10%. Why does hanging curtains and putting foam on the walls make the muddy sound clearer?
choices: They stop the speaker from producing sound, so the hall becomes silent
They reflect more sound back to the speaker, so the voice is stronger
They make sound travel faster, so the 0.07 s delay disappears
They absorb much of the sound energy, so there are fewer repeated reflections and the reverberation is shorter
quiz.rationale: Soft materials absorb sound energy instead of reflecting it. With less energy reflected back and forth, the overlapping reflections die away quickly and the sound is clearer. The delay itself and the source do not change.
quiz.placement: Design a noise-reduction treatment for the Kisumu hall

quiz.prompt: At Hell's Gate, a learner shouts at a cliff and hears the echo 0.50 s later. The speed of sound is 340 m/s. How far away is the cliff?
quiz.rationale: The sound travels to the cliff and back, so d = vt/2 = 340 × 0.50 / 2 = 85 m. Using 170 m forgets that this is a round trip.
quiz.placement: Final DQB review: 'Why is there a delay?' answered by t = 2d/v

quiz.prompt: On open school grounds, the nearest large hard wall is 300 m away, so the reflected sound returns after about 1.76 s. Yet the learner hears no echo. What is the best explanation?
choices: Sound travels more slowly over open ground, so it never returns
The delay is too long for the human ear to detect any sound
The sound spreads out over a large area and the grass and bushes absorb it, so the returning sound is too faint
The delay is shorter than 0.1 s, so the echo merges with the shout
quiz.rationale: A longer delay does not mean a stronger echo. Strength depends on how much energy is reflected. Spreading and absorption by grass (about 10% reflected) leave the returning sound too faint to hear.
quiz.placement: Step 2: final model, site D Nairobi open grounds

quiz.prompt: A sound ray hits a hard, smooth wall so that the angle between the ray and the normal is 30°. What is the angle between the reflected ray and the normal?
quiz.rationale: The law of reflection says the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal. So the reflected angle is also 30°.
quiz.placement: Step 2: final model showing angle of incidence i equal to angle of reflection r from the normal

quiz.prompt: Which statement best completes the Final Explanation of why some places give an echo and others do not?
choices: Soft surfaces such as foam and grass reflect sound best, so they give the clearest echoes
An echo is heard only when the reflector is at least 17 m away and reflects enough sound energy
The longer the delay, the stronger the echo, so far walls always give the loudest echo
An echo is heard whenever sound meets any surface, whatever the distance
quiz.rationale: A distinct echo needs a delay of at least 0.1 s, which means a reflector at least 17 m away. The surface must also reflect enough energy, as hard smooth surfaces do. Soft surfaces absorb sound.
quiz.placement: Step 5: individual Final Explanation using claim, evidence and reasoning
